source.title: Noisy Early Stopping for Noisy Labels

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests how noisy-label corruption relates to clean test accuracy and early stopping, but does not measure random-label memorization or training error.
record.gate_note: The study trains classifiers on several noisy-label datasets and reports clean test accuracy and early-stopping outcomes. It does not report whether training error reaches zero on randomly labeled data. Cited claims about memorization are not this study’s results.
record.test_reason: The study evaluates early stopping as a mitigation for noisy-label overfitting. Its own outcomes are held-out accuracy, model-selection performance and held-out prediction trajectories. It does not measure training-label memorization, fitting time, or the order of learning clean versus corrupted training labels. These results therefore do not test V1–V6; the record's T2 classification and V4 tested status should be removed.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is substantially accurate. The authors find that noisy validation accuracy enables near-optimal early stopping across the tested datasets, losses and noise types. Their general theoretical guarantee applies to uniform symmetric class-preserving noise; effectiveness beyond that setting remains incompletely explained, with a partial explanation explored in Appendix F. They qualify the empirical conclusion by the class-preserving assumption, closed-set noise and sufficient validation data.
record.recipe_differences: Studies early stopping on datasets with synthetic label noise, comparing noisy validation accuracy with clean validation accuracy and no early stopping; it does not reproduce random-label memorization experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that NES and clean early stopping diverge when noise ceases to be class-preserving. Performance also varies by dataset, loss function and noise type.

fits_no_version.finding: NES overlaps or exceeds clean early stopping within the reported uncertainty intervals in 93% of settings and outperforms training without early stopping in 75% (Table 1).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Noisy validation accuracy often permits effective early stopping for neural classifiers trained with label noise.

fits_no_version.finding: Figure 4 shows alignment between noisy and clean early stopping below class-preserving thresholds, followed by divergence when that condition fails.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The effectiveness of noisy early stopping depends on the label-noise structure, including whether it preserves the dominant class.

fits_no_version.finding: Appendix F.5 and Figures 13–15 show held-out incorrect-class prediction proportions reaching minima around the same early epochs in ternary MNIST and five-class CIFAR.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Approximately simultaneous minima in held-out error components can explain alignment between noisy and clean accuracy peaks.

record.problems: The tested outcomes do not include training error, so they cannot establish whether networks fit noisy or random training labels. Figure 4 values are presented graphically without recoverable numbers. Table 1 averages over three runs and reports standard deviations, but covers many dataset, method and loss combinations.
record.rows_left_out: No rows retained: the reported outcomes concern clean test accuracy and early-stopping comparisons, while V4 also requires evidence about training-set fit. Figure 4 reports noise-rate curves without recoverable numeric values; Table 1 reports fixed-noise results across datasets, six loss functions and three methods, but none reports training error.

untested.parts: Near-zero training error on completely random labels, chance test performance, and unchanged architecture and training hyperparameters.
Relative time to fit true and random labels, and convergence slowdown with increasing corruption.
Training-set fit on shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels and Gaussian-noise inputs.

Perfect training-set fit across corruption levels together with steadily increasing test error toward chance. Figure 4 reports test accuracy after early stopping, without establishing training-set interpolation.
Whether weight decay, dropout and augmentation prevent random-label fitting, and whether removing them harms true-label generalization.
Whether shared real-label patterns are fitted before noisy training labels are memorized. Held-out accuracy and g-vector trajectories do not distinguish these training-label learning processes.

record.verdict_notes: No extracted rows require correction. Keeping the row set empty is appropriate for these claim versions. Declining held-out accuracy during training does not establish memorization of corrupted training labels, and the absence of training-error measurements is not evidence against the claims.

versions.untested_parts: Whether standard networks fit completely random labels to near-zero training error, with test error at chance and without changes to architecture or training hyperparameters.
Training-time cost of fitting random labels and how convergence time changes with the fraction of corrupted labels.
Fitting shuffled-pixel, permuted-pixel or Gaussian-noise inputs.

The paper reports clean test accuracy across noise levels and describes NES versus clean early stopping, but does not report training-set error across those noise levels. Figure 4 contains curves without recoverable numeric values; the table reports separate results for many dataset, loss and method combinations, which are not extracted here.
Whether weight decay, dropout or augmentation affect fitting random labels, or whether removing them harms true-label generalization.
Whether real-label patterns are learned before noisy or random labels.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
